title: The Civil Rights Movement
summary: Weigh what changed, what changed slowly, and what stayed the same across the Civil Rights Movement (1954–1968), and judge whether it was a true turning point.
challenge: Between 1954 and 1968, courts, laws, and mass movements dismantled the legal framework of segregation. But law on paper and life on the ground are not the same thing. Compare before, during, and after — then judge: was this era a genuine turning point in U.S. history, or the acceleration of a longer struggle?

before: Jim Crow laws and legally enforced segregation across the South
Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) 'separate but equal' doctrine
Systematic Black disenfranchisement — poll taxes, literacy tests, white primaries, intimidation
during: Legal strategy in the courts (NAACP Legal Defense Fund; Brown v. Board, 1954)
Nonviolent direct action — boycotts, sit-ins, Freedom Rides, marches
Grassroots organizing (SCLC, SNCC, CORE, NAACP) and youth leadership
Federal intervention prompted by protest and violence (Little Rock; Selma → Voting Rights Act)
after: Landmark federal law: Civil Rights Act (1964), Voting Rights Act (1965), Fair Housing Act (1968)
A sharp rise in Black voter registration and officeholding, especially in the South
Persistent limits: de facto segregation, economic inequality, and later rollbacks (Shelby County v. Holder, 2013)
mapData.sigKey: The legal status of segregation and voting: federal law made de jure segregation and discriminatory voting tests illegal.
mapData.gradKey: Actual desegregation of schools and public life, and the growth of Black political participation — over years, not overnight.
mapData.sameKey: De facto segregation and deep economic disparities in housing, wealth, and schooling persisted despite legal change.
mapData.whyKey: Why did some conditions change quickly (the law on paper) while others changed slowly or barely at all (everyday economic and residential realities)? What is the difference between de jure and de facto change?

comparePromptKeys: Compare your ledgers with a partner. Did you sort the same items into 'changed' vs. 'stayed the same'?

conclusionKey: Was 1954–1968 a genuine turning point, or the acceleration of a longer struggle? Use evidence from at least two sources, cite specific laws or events, and address at least one way change was incomplete.

ace.articulateKey: Explain the difference between de jure and de facto change using one example.
ace.connectKey: Connect a protest or event 'during' the movement to a law that came 'after' it.
ace.extendKey: Apply the continuity-and-change lens to a rights movement happening today. What has changed, and what has not?

teacherText.keyideas: The movement changed the law decisively (Brown; the 1964, 1965, and 1968 Acts) while everyday desegregation and economic equality changed slowly or remained out of reach. The de jure / de facto distinction is the analytical heart of the lesson: legal change and lived change are related but not identical. Present tactics (litigation and nonviolent direct action) and federal responses as prompted by grassroots pressure.
teacherText.misconceptions:
• Laws did not instantly end segregation; enforcement and de facto segregation persisted.
• The movement was a broad, organized, grassroots effort, not the work of a few famous individuals alone.
• Gains were later contested (e.g., Shelby County v. Holder, 2013, weakened the Voting Rights Act).
teacherText.vocabulary: de jure, de facto, segregation, disenfranchisement, nonviolent direct action, Jim Crow, Brown v. Board, filibuster.
teacherText.context: Brown v. Board (1954); Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56); Little Rock (1957); Greensboro sit-ins (1960); March on Washington (1963); Civil Rights Act (1964); Voting Rights Act (1965); Fair Housing Act (1968).
